sections.h2: Can a squatter take ownership of a house in Iowa?
sections.html:
Only through adverse possession, and Iowa courts make the claimant prove a long list of facts over at least ten years. The doctrine is strictly construed, and a claim must be established by "clear and positive proof" (Olsen v. Hennings, Iowa Court of Appeals, 2012).

Moving into an empty house and staying a few months comes nowhere close. The ten-year period applies to the claim itself. A short-term occupant creates a removal problem instead, which the Code handles through a separate fast court process described below.

The claimant must show hostile, actual, open, exclusive and continuous possession, under a claim of right or color of title, for at least ten years. That is the list the court laid out in Olsen v. Hennings.

ElementPlain meaning in Iowa decisions
HostileContrary to the true legal title. It does not require ill will or bad faith.
Actual and openThe claimant really uses the land the way an owner would, and anyone could see it.
ExclusiveHeld to the exclusion of the true owner.
ContinuousWithout a break across the full period.
Claim of right or color of titleOnly one of the two is needed. Color of title is something that looks like title but is not.
Ten yearsTied to the ten-year limit for actions to recover real property (Iowa Code 614.1).

The cases build the adverse possession elements around that ten-year window. The claimant carries the burden at every step.

sections.h2: What a successful Iowa claim looks like
sections.html:
Reported Iowa wins often involve a neighbor and a strip of land. One example is Summit Veterinary Services v. Tindle, decided by the Iowa Court of Appeals in 2017.

  • A couple bought their home in 1977 and paved a driveway with asphalt.
  • In 1979 the owners of a neighboring clinic built a fence along the south side of the driveway, and the husband helped build and maintain it.
  • The couple treated the land north of the fence as theirs, adding carports in 2002 and 2006.
  • In 2015 a new clinic owner had the property surveyed and sued to quiet title. The couple counterclaimed, and the courts ruled for them.

Two lessons for owners. A mistaken belief about ownership did not defeat the claim, because the court saw it as good faith in asserting a right. And a claim of right can be shown by using and improving land as an owner would, without paying rent or acknowledging anyone else's title.

A boundary dispute is about where a line runs between two owners, and Iowa has its own court procedure in chapter 650. An owner of land with lost, destroyed or disputed boundaries may sue in district court in the county where the land lies.

A party may plead that the boundaries were recognized and acquiesced in for ten consecutive years (section 650.6). The court may appoint disinterested surveyors to locate the corners. Their report is due within sixty days of appointment, with twenty days afterward to file exceptions (sections 650.7, 650.11 and 650.12). Neighbors can also fix a line by a signed, acknowledged and recorded written agreement with a plat (section 650.17).

If an old fence or driveway edge is the problem, this chapter usually fits better than an eviction case.

sections.h2: How an Iowa owner removes someone with no right to be there
sections.html:
The main tool is forcible entry and detainer, a summary court action under chapter 648. It covers entry by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth, holdovers after a lease, nonpayment of rent, possession after a foreclosure or execution sale, and possession after a valid tax deed (section 648.1).

  • Notice: three days' written notice to quit before suing on any ground except forcible entry by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth (section 648.3). Serve it personally, through a signed acknowledgment from a resident aged 18 or older, or by posting on the main door plus regular and certified mail.
  • Hearing: no later than 8 days from filing, or 15 if the plaintiff asks or consents to a later date (section 648.5).
  • Judgment: if the defendant is found guilty, the court orders removal, and an execution for removal issues within 3 days (section 648.22).
  • Execution time: an order for removal may be carried out only in the daytime (section 648.20).

Timing matters. If the defendant keeps peaceable possession for thirty days with the plaintiff's knowledge after the cause of action arises, that bars the forcible entry proceeding (section 648.18). Chapter 648 also leaves room for a separate trespass suit or other ways of testing property rights (section 648.17).

sections.h2: Trespass after being told to leave
sections.html:
In many cases, yes. Under section 716.7, trespass includes entering or remaining on property without justification after being told to leave or stay out.

The request can come from the owner, a lessee, a person in lawful possession, their agent or employee, or a peace officer or magistrate. It can be given personally, orally or in writing, or through a valid court order under chapter 236. A printed notice conspicuously posted at the main entrance counts too. The text carves out no exception for vacant buildings, and the general definition of property covers any building or structure, public or private.

If you find an unknown person inside, write down when and how you gave notice. That record helps with a police report and a later court filing.

A person under a legal disability gets extra time to start an action. Under section 614.8, a minor has one year after reaching majority, and a person with mental illness has one year after the disability ends.

Chapter 614 also has older-claim rules that touch title. Section 614.17A bars an action against a record holder in possession if the claim is more than ten years old and the holder has held the chain of title for over ten years, unless the claimant filed a written statement with the county recorder within ten years of when the claim arose. A person with an unbroken record chain of forty years or more has marketable record title (section 614.31).

These rules are technical. A title examiner or attorney can say how they apply to a specific parcel.

sections.h2: Vacant houses, and whether you can still sell
sections.html:
Start by documenting the property and sending written notice, then use the chapter 648 process if someone remains. Keep dates, photographs and copies of everything you serve.

An occupancy problem does not block a sale, but it affects price and timing. A title search can turn up recorded claims, and a buyer who wants a fast closing has to decide how much risk to take on. Cash Home Buyers buys Iowa houses as-is, including ones with occupants or title questions, and we would look at the facts before making any offer. For a legal read on your own situation, see an Iowa attorney.

faqs.q: How long does adverse possession take in Iowa?
faqs.a: At least ten years of continuous possession that meets every element. The period tracks the ten-year limit for actions to recover real property in Iowa Code 614.1.

faqs.q: Does paying property taxes on land help an adverse possession claim?
faqs.a: Courts weigh the stated elements and the overall proof. An attorney can tell you how a court in your county has treated tax payments.

faqs.q: Can I evict a squatter in Iowa without going to court?
faqs.a: No. The Iowa Code provides a court process, forcible entry and detainer, for removal. A notice to quit comes first on most grounds.

faqs.q: How long is the notice to quit in Iowa?
faqs.a: Three days of written notice, except when the claim is forcible entry by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth. Mailed notice is complete four days after deposit.

faqs.q: Can an owner lose land to a neighbor through a fence line?
faqs.a: It can happen. Iowa courts found adverse possession of a strip along a fence line in the 2017 Summit Veterinary case, and chapter 650 allows a boundary to be fixed after ten consecutive years of acquiescence.
